title: Anil Grover vs Ms Kortek Electronics India Ltd. Ors on 22 December, 2025

IN THE COURT OF JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE FIRST CLASS (NI ACT-02), SOUTH EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURT COMPLEX, NEW DELHI (Presided over by Ms. Shruti Sharma-I) DLSE020008702013 Criminal Complaint No. 614872/2016 Anil Grover ........... Date of institution 03.10.2013 G. Date of pronouncement 22.12.2025 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.1/27 SHRUTI Date: SHARMA 2025.12.22 17:00:45 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. JUDGMENT 1. This Court, by the present detailed judgment, adjudicates the complaint instituted by Sh. Anil Grover proprietor of M/s Micro Devices Inc., a reputed manufacturer and supplier of professional electronic components (hereinafter "Complainant"). The complaint targets M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. (Accused No. 1), a company represented by AR Sh. Navin Tiwari and its Director Sh. Y. M Yoon (now expired), for offences punishable under Section 138 r/w Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (" NI Act "). The prosecution stems from the dishonour of a specific cheque issued by the Accused(s) in purported discharge of a legally enforceable debt cheque bearing no. 034854 dated 28.06.2013 for Rs. 4,11,535/- drawn on Citi Bank, NA, New Delhi. The cheque, handed over as payment of an accumulated liability from goods supplied, was presented for encashment via ICICI Bank, Jhandewalan Extension, New Delhi, but returned unpaid on 20.08.2013 with the bank endorsement "refer to drawer". Despite statutory legal demand notice and the Accused's failure to remit payment within the prescribed 15-day window, the cause of action crystallized, warranting invocation of NI Act 's penal provisions. 2. It is the case of the complainant that the complainant, Shri Anil Grover, proprietor of M/s Micro Devices Inc., is engaged in the business of sale and supply of professional electronic components and carries on business from Nehru Place, New Delhi. It is the case of the complainant that accused no.1, M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd., a company incorporated under the Companies Act , through accused nos. 2 to 4, who are its Managing Director/Directors and in charge of and responsible for the day-to-day affairs of the company, placed a purchase order bearing No. PO/STO/1213/2552 dated 23.03.2013 for supply of certain electronic items. Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.2/27 SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:00:46 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. 3. Pursuant to the said purchase order, the complainant supplied the ordered goods to the accused vide Invoice No. E-030 dated 22.04.2013 for a total amount of Rs. 4,11,535/-. The goods were duly received and acknowledged by the accused. It is averred that the said amount became legally payable by the accused to the complainant towards the price of the goods supplied. 4. In discharge of the aforesaid liability, accused no.1 company, through accused no.2, issued cheque bearing No. 034854 dated 28.06.2013 for a sum of Rs. 4,11,535/- drawn on Citi Bank, NA, New Delhi, in favour of the complainant, with an assurance that the same would be honoured on presentation. 5. The complainant presented the said cheque for encashment through its banker, ICICI Bank, Nehru Place Branch, New Delhi. To the Complainant's profound dismay, the cheque dishonoured upon presentment, with the remark "Refer to Drawer" --a fact corroborated by original return memo. Preceding assurances from the Accused notwithstanding, post-dishonour communications yielded only temporizing excuses and hollow pledges of imminent settlement. This pattern of evasion underscored a lack of genuine intent to honour the instruments. 6. Adhering scrupulously to Section 138 NI Act, the Complainant's counsel dispatched a comprehensive legal demand notice dated 24.08.2013 via speed posts and courier to the Accused's declared addresses. The notice categorically demanded repayment of the cheque amount within 15 days of receipt. Postal receipts confirm dispatch, with deemed service thereafter. The Accused's resounding silence--no payment, no rebuttal--fortified the presumption of liability under Section 139 NI Act. 7. The deliberate issuance of cheque foreseeably dishonour, and defiant non- compliance post-notice collectively constitute wilful default. This sequence repudiates any defence of bona fides, portraying calculated circumvention of a proven commercial obligation, squarely indictable under SectionDigitally 138 NIsigned Act. by SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.3/27 SHRUTI Date: SHARMA 2025.12.22 17:00:48 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. The Complainant's unimpugned averments and documents establish the foundational ingredients: a cheque issued in debt discharge, dishonour, and failed notice redressal. 8. Upon a careful perusal of the material placed on record along with the complaint, and after due examination of the complainant by way of pre- summoning evidence in accordance with the mandate of Section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, this Court was satisfied that a prima facie case was made out against the accused for the commission of an offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The evidence adduced at the pre-summoning stage sufficiently disclosed the existence of a legally enforceable liability and the issuance of the cheque in question by the accused towards its discharge, followed by its dishonour. Accordingly, vide order dated 18.11.2015, this Court was pleased to take cognizance of the offence and summoned the accused to face trial for the alleged dishonour of cheque issued in discharge of a debt or liability, as contemplated under the statutory scheme of the NI Act . 9. The accused no. 1 company appeared through its AR on 21.07.2016 with counsel. Subsequently, upon satisfaction that a prima facie case existed warranting trial, this Court proceeded to frame notice under Section 251 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 ( CrPC ), which was duly served upon the accused company through its AR on 18.01.2018. Upon being apprised of the substance of accusation, including the specific allegations pertaining to issuance and dishonour of the cheque in question, the accused company pleaded not guilty and claimed trial, thereby necessitating the recording of evidence in the matter in accordance with law. 10. Thereafter, in support of its case, the complainant adopted his pre-summoning evidence and tendered his evidence affidavit. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. examined himself only as witness CW-1. CW1/Sh. Anil Grover entered the witness box and relied on the following documents in support of his case:- Sr. Exhibits Particulars No. 1. Ex.CW-1/A Evidence by way of Affidavit 2. Ex.CW-1/1 Purchase Order PO/STO/1213/2552 dated 23.03.2013. 3. Ex.CW-1/2 Invoice E-030 dated 22.04.2013 4. Ex.CW-1/3 Original Cheque No. 034854 dated 28.06.2013. 5. Ex.CW-1/4 Cheque returning memo dated 20.08.2013 with remarks 'refer to drawer'. 6. Ex.CW-1/5 Copy of Legal Demand notice dated 24.08.2013. 7. Ex.CW-1/6(Colly) Speed post receipts. 8. Ex.CW-1/7(Colly.) Courier receipts 9. Ex.CW-1/8(Colly.) Tracking reports 10. Ex.CW-1/9 Complaint u/s 138 NI Act. 7. The aforesaid stage was thereafter followed by an extensive examination-in-chief of CW-1, who was subjected to a detailed and searching cross-examination on behalf of the accused. Upon completion of such cross-examination, and no further questions remaining to be put to the witness by either side, CW-1 was formally discharged by the Court on 02.06.2022, in accordance with law. 8. Upon completion of the complainant evidence and as the complainant did not wish to examine any other witness, hence the matter fixed for recording of statement of accused u/s 313 CrPC and subsequent to the conclusion of the complainant's Digitally signed Page no.5/27 by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:00:52 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. evidence, and in compliance with the procedural mandate under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the statement of the accused through AR was recorded by the Court on 11.07.2022, thereby affording it an opportunity to personally explain the incriminating circumstances appearing against it in the prosecution evidence. 9. Thereafter, the accused company was afforded a full and fair opportunity to lead evidence in defense. The AR of the accused entered the witness box as DW-1/Sh. Navin Tiwari who produced Ex.DW-1/A ie. the Board Resolution in his favour. DW-1 was thoroughly examined in chief, cross examined by the complainant and discharged on 22.03.2023. DE was closed as the defense did not wish to examine any other witness in support. Thus, the matter was accordingly directed to proceed to the stage of final arguments. Final Arguments 10. Thereafter, this Court heard and considered the final arguments advanced on behalf of both the parties on 21.11.2025. Upon conclusion of the said submissions, the matter was reserved for pronouncement of judgment. 11. Learned counsel for the complainant has argued that the complainant has successfully proved all the essential ingredients of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. It is submitted that pursuant to the purchase order dated 23.03.2013 (Ex. CW1/1), the complainant duly supplied goods to accused no.1 company vide Invoice No. E-030 dated 22.04..2013 for a sum of Rs. 4,11,535 (Ex. CW1/2), which were received and acknowledged by the accused. 12. It is contended that in discharge of the said legally enforceable liability, the accused issued cheque bearing No. 034854 dated 28.06.2013 for Rs. 4,11,535/- (Ex. CW1/3), which upon presentation was dishonoured vide return memo dated 20.08.2013 (Ex. CW1/4) for the reason "refer to drawer". Thereafter, a statutory legal demand notice dated 24.08.2013 (Ex. CW1/5) was duly issued and served Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.6/27 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:00:54 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. upon the accused through speed post and courier, as proved by postal receipts and tracking reports (Ex. CW1/6 to Ex. CW1/8 colly). Despite service, the accused failed to make payment within the statutory period, and hence, the present complaint was filed within limitation. 13. It is further argued that the defence taken by the accused has been wholly inconsistent and contradictory at different stages of the trial. At the stage of notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused claimed that the goods were defective and therefore, the cheque was not cleared. However, during cross-examination of CW-1 and later in the statement under Section 313 CrPC, the accused admitted that goods may have been received and further took a stand that payment of the entire liability had already been made. Such shifting stands, according to the complainant, demolish the credibility of the defence and show that the accused has made false statements on oath. 14. The complainant further relies upon the testimony of DW-1, Sh. Navin Tiwari, who admitted issuance of C-Form (Ex. DW1/X1) containing details of the very invoice in question and also identified his signatures thereon. It is argued that issuance of C-Forms and endorsement of Form ST-38 on the invoice, coupled with the stamp of the accused company on Ex. CW1/2, clearly establishes that the goods were in fact received by accused no.1 company. It is submitted that C-Forms could not have been issued unless goods had been received, and hence, the defence of non-supply stands falsified. 15. It is contended that in view of the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act, the cheque is presumed to have been issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt, and the accused has miserably failed to rebut the said presumption by any cogent or credible evidence. On the contrary, the defence evidence is self- contradictory and evasive. It is further argued that service of legal demand notice stands duly proved, especially in view of the admission of the accused under Section Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.7/27 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:00:56 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. 313 CrPC that the address mentioned on the notice is the correct address of the factory. Hence, the plea of non-service of notice is untenable. 16. Learned counsel has also relied upon Section 141 of the NI Act to submit that since the offence has been committed by the company, all persons who were in charge of and responsible for the conduct of its business at the relevant time are vicariously liable. It is argued that accused nos. 2 to 4, being Directors/Managing Director, were responsible for the affairs of accused no.1 company, and therefore, are liable to be prosecuted and punished, though proceedings against accused no.2 stand abated due to his death. Lastly, it is submitted that the complainant has proved that: (i) the cheque was issued towards a legally enforceable liability, (ii) the cheque was dishonoured, (iii) despite service of legal demand notice, no payment was made within the statutory period, and (iv) the complaint has been filed within limitation. Hence, all the ingredients of Section 138 NI Act are fulfilled. Accordingly, it is prayed that the accused be convicted and punished in accordance with law. 17. Per contra, Learned Counsel for the accused contended that the present complaint is vitiated both on factual and legal grounds, and that the complainant has failed to establish the foundational ingredients necessary to attract penal liability under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Learned counsel for the accused has argued that the present complaint is false, frivolous and an abuse of the process of law, and that no offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is made out against the accused. 18. It is contended that the cheque in question was not issued in discharge of any legally enforceable debt or liability, but was given merely as a security cheque in the course of business dealings between the parties. It is argued that the complainant has misused the said cheque, despite there being no subsisting liability on the date of its presentation. The defence has further submitted that the complainant failed to prove actual supply of goods as alleged. According to the accused, no material was Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.8/27 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:01:00 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. supplied pursuant to the invoice relied upon by the complainant, and therefore, no liability arose against the accused company. 19. It is also argued that the statutory legal demand notice was not duly served upon the accused, and therefore, the mandatory requirement under proviso (b) to Section 138 of the NI Act has not been complied with, rendering the complaint not maintainable. It is argued that the presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act are rebuttable, and in the facts of the present case, the accused has raised a probable defence by showing serious inconsistencies in the complainant's version and by disputing the existence of any legally enforceable debt. Hence, the burden has shifted back upon the complainant, who has failed to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. 20. Lastly, it is contended that the complainant has not approached the Court with clean hands and has suppressed material facts. Accordingly, the accused prays that he be acquitted of the offence under Section 138 of the NI Act. Legal Analysis & Findings:- 21. I have heard at considerable length the detailed arguments advanced by the learned counsel appearing for the complainant as well as the learned counsel representing the accused. Their respective submissions have been carefully analysed in the context of the factual matrix and the legal principles applicable to the case. This Court has also undertaken a thorough and meticulous scrutiny of the entire judicial record, which includes the contents of the complaint, the affidavits and supporting documents annexed thereto, the oral testimonies of the complainant's and the defence witnesses, if any, recorded during the course of trial, and all exhibits relied upon by the respective parties. Each piece of evidence has been examined individually as well as in conjunction with the other evidence on record so as to assess its evidentiary value, credibility, and probative strength. The rival submissions have been objectively evaluated against the backdrop of the statutory Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.9/27 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:01:02 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. framework and the well-settled legal position governing proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The Court has, therefore, endeavored to reach a reasoned and just determination by adopting a holistic and balanced appreciation of the evidence and circumstances presented before it. 22. Before embarking upon a discussion on the merits of the present case, it is considered apposite to first delineate the legal framework governing the offence of dishonour of cheque, as encapsulated under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The legislative intent behind enacting Section 138 is to instill greater financial discipline and sanctity in contractual obligations by deterring the issuance of cheques without sufficient funds or without adequate arrangements with the banker. The provision prescribes penal consequences in the event of dishonor of a cheque on grounds of insufficiency of funds or if the amount exceeds the arrangement with the bank, thereby recognizing the cheque as a legitimate instrument of payment in the eyes of the law. 23. In order to fasten criminal liability upon an accused under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, it is incumbent upon the complainant to plead and prove the existence of certain foundational ingredients through the averments made in the complaint and the evidence led during the course of trial. The essential ingredients that must be cumulatively satisfied are as follows: a. That the accused must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him with a banker, for the payment of a certain sum of money to another person, and such payment must have been intended for the discharge, in whole or in part, of a legally enforceable debt or other liability; b. That the said cheque must have been presented to the bank within a period of three months from the date on which it was drawn, or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.10/27 SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:01:06 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. c. That upon such presentation, the cheque must have been returned unpaid by the bank, either due to insufficiency of funds in the drawer's account or because the amount exceeded the arrangement made by the drawer with the bank; d. That the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque must have issued a written statutory demand notice to the drawer, seeking payment of the cheque amount, within 30 days from the date of receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque unpaid; e. That the drawer of the cheque, despite the receipt of such legal notice, failed to make payment of the cheque amount to the payee or holder in due course within 15 days from the date of such receipt. 24. Only upon proof of the aforementioned ingredients does the offence under Section 138 stand attracted, subject to the operation of statutory presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act. These presumptions, however, are rebuttable and impose a reverse burden upon the accused to dislodge the same on a preponderance of probabilities. 25. It is also pertinent to note that, as per the Explanation appended to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the expression "debt or other liability" refers exclusively to a legally enforceable debt or other liability. This legal clarification is of critical significance, as it makes clear that mere issuance of a cheque is not sufficient to attract penal liability under the statute. The dishonoured cheque must have been issued in discharge of a debt or liability which is subsisting and legally enforceable at the time of its issuance. A cheque issued as a gift, donation, or towards a time-barred or non-existent liability will not fall within the purview of Section 138 . Thus, the complainant must establish that at the time the cheque was drawn, there existed a valid and enforceable obligation in law for which the cheque Digitally was issued. signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.11/27 SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:01:13 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. 26. It is well-settled in law that the aforementioned ingredients must co-exist and be satisfied cumulatively in order to constitute the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The absence or non-fulfilment of even one of these statutory requirements is fatal to the prosecution's case and would disentitle the complainant from invoking penal liability against the drawer of the cheque. 27. CW-1, Shri Anil Grover, proprietor of M/s Micro Devices Inc., tendered his pre- summoning affidavit Ex. CW-1/A as his post-summoning evidence and relied upon documents Ex. CW-1/1 to Ex. CW-1/9. He deposed that accused no.1 company, through accused nos. 2 to 4, placed a purchase order dated 23.03.2013 (Ex. CW-1/1) for supply of electronic components. Pursuant thereto, he supplied the goods vide Invoice No. E-030 dated 22.04.2013 for an amount of Rs.4,11,535 (Ex. CW-1/2), which were duly received and acknowledged by the accused. 28. He further deposed that in discharge of the said liability, accused no.1 issued cheque bearing No. 034854 dated 28.06.2013 for Rs. 4,11,535/- drawn on Citi Bank (Ex. CW-1/3), which on presentation was dishonoured vide return memo dated 20.08.2013 for the reason "refer to drawer" (Ex. CW-1/4). Thereafter, legal demand notice dated 24.08.2013 was issued and served upon the accused (Ex. CW-1/5 to Ex. CW-1/8), but despite service, no payment was made. He proved the complaint as Ex. CW-1/9. 29. During cross-examination, CW-1 stated that he had been dealing with the accused company since 2011-12 and that earlier transactions had been duly settled, and the present complaint pertains only to the invoice and cheque in question. He admitted that he had not filed a statement of account regarding previous dealings but volunteered that no amount was outstanding in respect thereof. He also stated that VAT returns pertaining to the transaction in question had been filed and exhibited Digitally as Ex. CW-1/10DX. signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: Page no.12/27 2025.12.22 17:01:16 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. 30. CW-1 admitted that he had not filed company master data to show that accused no.2 was a Director at the relevant time, but stated that the cheque in question bears the signatures of accused no.2. He deposed that he did not remember who handed over the cheque to him, and that he verified later that the signatures on the cheque were of accused no.2. He further stated that the goods were sent through transport as per instructions of the accused and that the invoice Ex. CW-1/2 bears the stamp of the accused company and signatures of the person who received the goods, though he could not name the said person. He denied the suggestion that the accused company did not receive the goods. 31. CW-1 admitted that Ex. CW-1/2 does not bear his signatures and that the purchase order Ex. CW-1/1 was a printout taken from email received by his sales department. He stated that the invoices were filled by his employee but denied that he had no knowledge of the same. He also tendered certificates under Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act as Ex. CW-1/DX1 and Ex. CW-1/DX2 and admitted that the same were not notarised but were filed with supporting affidavit. 32. He stated that apart from the present case, one more complaint under Section 138 NI Act was pending against the accused and that no other payment was due except in those two cases. He denied the suggestions that the invoices were fake, that no goods were supplied, that the cheque was not issued towards liability, or that he was deposing falsely. After his examination, CW-1 closed his evidence 33. Insofar as the statutory ingredients (b), (c), (d), and (e) under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are concerned--namely, (b) the presentation of the cheque within its validity period, (c) its dishonour by the bank due to the reason mentioned in the return memo, (d) the issuance of a legal demand notice within 30 days of receiving intimation of dishonour, and (e) the drawer's failure to make payment within 15 days of receipt of the said notice--this Court finds that the complainant has successfully discharged the burden of proof in respect thereof. These facts stand duly established through unimpeached documentary evidence Digitally signed by Page no.13/27 SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:01:18 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. placed on record, which includes the original cheque, the cheque return memo, the legal demand notice, the postal receipts confirming dispatch. There is no rebuttal to the presumption of service, and hence, the requirements under clauses (b) to (e) of Section 138 stand conclusively fulfilled. 34. It is also not in dispute that the accused failed to make payment of the cheque amount to the complainant within the statutory period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the legal demand notice. The record clearly reflects that the notice was dispatched to the accused, as evidenced by the postal receipts placed on record. Hence, service of the legal notice stands proved. Despite being afforded the statutory opportunity under the mandate of Section 138 of the NI Act, the accused did not tender the cheque amount within the prescribed period of 15 days, thereby fulfilling the last statutory condition for attracting penal liability under the said provision. 35. The Court shall now proceed to examine the most crucial ingredient under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which constitutes the very foundation of the present prosecution--namely, whether the impugned cheque was issued by the accused in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or other liability. This aspect is of paramount significance, as the existence of such a liability is the sine qua non for attracting the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act. 36. In this background, this Court now undertakes a detailed and careful evaluation of the rival contentions and the evidence on record, to determine whether the said essential ingredient stands proved to the requisite standard in the present matter. 37. It is well-settled that once the complainant establishes that the cheque was drawn by the accused and that it was returned unpaid, a presumption arises under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Act that the cheque was issued for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. The initial burden upon the complainant is merely to prove the foundational facts--namely, the execution and dishonour of the cheque. Once this is done, the burden shifts upon the accused to rebut the presumption. Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.14/27 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:01:20 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. Such rebuttal may be established either by leading positive evidence or by pointing out inconsistencies, improbabilities, or material contradictions in the complainant's case, which may raise a reasonable doubt as to the existence of the alleged liability. 38. For ready reference, the relevant provisions are reproduced as under:  Section 118(a) , NI Act - "Presumptions as to negotiable instruments: Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: (a) of consideration--that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration."  Section 139 , NI Act - "Presumption in favour of holder: It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 39. This presumption, though statutory, is rebuttable in nature. The law places the initial evidentiary burden upon the accused to dislodge this presumption by raising a probable defence. It is now well-settled that the accused is not required to rebut the presumption beyond reasonable doubt; rather, the standard of rebuttal is that of preponderance of probabilities. The accused may discharge this burden either by adducing direct evidence or by relying on material inconsistencies, improbabilities, or contradictions in the complainant's case, elicited during cross-examination or otherwise. However, unless such rebuttal is successfully established, the presumption continues to operate in favour of the complainant. 40. This is a classic illustration of the principle of 'reverse onus' in operation, wherein the statutory scheme obligates the accused to rebut the presumption in favour of the Digitally complainant by leading what may be termed as 'negative evidence'. The signed accusedbyis SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.15/27 SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:01:22 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. not required to affirmatively prove a particular fact; rather, he must bring on record material to demonstrate the non-existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. 41. Since this reverse burden deviates from the general principle of criminal jurisprudence--namely, the presumption of innocence in favour of the accused-- the law has correspondingly tempered the standard of rebuttal. Recognizing the inherent difficulty in leading negative evidence, the standard prescribed is not that of proof beyond reasonable doubt, but of preponderance of probabilities. As held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sangappa v. Mohan, (2010) 11 SCC 441, the accused need not conclusively disprove the existence of consideration or liability; it is sufficient if he can raise a probable defence which renders the existence of such liability doubtful or improbable in the mind of the Court. 42. In order to discharge the burden cast upon him under the reverse onus clause, the accused is required to either prove the non-existence of the alleged liability or demonstrate that the existence of such liability is so improbable or doubtful that a prudent person would conclude that no such obligation existed. This can be achieved by the accused either by leading direct evidence or relying upon circumstantial evidence in his defence. Alternatively, the accused may choose to effectively challenge the complainant's case by eliciting material contradictions or inconsistencies during cross-examination, thereby undermining the credibility of the prosecution's version. 43. If the accused succeeds in creating such a doubt, the burden then shifts back to the complainant, who must establish the existence of liability independent of the statutory presumptions. In such a scenario, the presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act would cease to operate in favour of the complainant and cannot be relied upon as conclusive proof. The complainant would then have to establish the liability on the strength of his own evidence. Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.16/27 SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:01:25 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. 44. In the light of the foregoing statutory provisions and the settled principles of law governing the operation and rebuttal of presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, this Court shall now proceed to critically examine the defence set up by the accused. The pivotal issue for consideration at this stage is whether the defence raised by the accused is plausible, probable, and legally sustainable--such as would be sufficient to rebut the presumption regarding the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. 45. The defence may be founded either on direct evidence adduced by the accused or may emerge from material inconsistencies, omissions, or inherent improbabilities discernible within the complainant's version, particularly as elicited during cross- examination. However, to succeed, the defence must be cogent enough to inspire confidence and must raise a credible doubt regarding the true purpose behind the issuance of the impugned cheque. Such vagueness and absence of particulars render the plea of a "security cheque" wholly unreliable and incapable of rebutting the statutory presumption in favour of the complainant. 67. Furthermore, the plea raised on behalf of the accused that the cheque in question had been issued merely as a "security instrument" is wholly untenable in law and cannot constitute a valid defence under the scheme of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 . The Supreme Court has consistently held that the nomenclature or description assigned to a cheque as "security" is of no consequence if, at the time of its presentation, a legally enforceable debt or liability is found to subsist. In Sripati Singh v. State of Jharkhand [(2021) 11 SCC 264], the Hon'ble Court repelled the argument that dishonour of a so-called security cheque is immune from the rigours of Section 138 NI Act, and emphatically reiterated that even a cheque given as Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.24/27 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.22 17:01:44 +0530 Ct case no. 614872/2016 Anil Grover Vs. M/s Kortek Electronics India Ltd. security will attract penal consequences if it is presented against an existing liability and is subsequently dishonoured. 68. Accordingly, what is material and determinative is not the description of the instrument as "security," but the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability on the date of its presentation. Once such liability is established, the dishonour of the cheque, irrespective of the purpose for which it was originally issued, would squarely fall within the ambit of Section 138 of the Act. Therefore, the defence advanced by the accused on this score is devoid of merit and deserves outright rejection. 69. Significantly, despite having received a copy of the complaint and having appeared before this Court since the year 2016, DW-1 has candidly admitted that no complaint, notice, or any other legal action was ever initiated against the complainant alleging misuse of the cheque in question, nor was any written demand ever made seeking return of the alleged security cheques. Such prolonged inaction on the part of the accused is wholly inconsistent with the conduct expected of a prudent person who genuinely believes that his cheque has been misused, and this omission, therefore, renders the defence plea of misuse not only improbable but wholly implausible. 70. At one stage, he has categorically stated that payment was not made as goods were defective; at another, he has equivocated by stating that goods "may have been received" while simultaneously claiming that full payment had already been made. Similarly, he has at one point denied the very purchase order forming the basis of the transaction, and yet, at another stage, has admitted issuance of the cheque in question. Such vacillation in the defence version, oscillating between denial of transaction, partial admission, and assertion of discharge of liability, strikes at the root of its credibility. The cumulative effect of the evidence on record unmistakably demonstrates that the accused has failed to rebut the statutory presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, even on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities. The defence put forth is founded merely on bald denials, shifting stands, and unsubstantiated assertions, unsupported by any cogent documentary or oral evidence. In contrast, the complainant's version stands firmly corroborated not only by contemporaneous documentary evidence but also by material admissions elicited from DW-1 during cross-examination. The defence has thus failed to probabilise its case or to cast any reasonable doubt on the existence of a legally enforceable liability. 72.
